data.title: Everything is made of atoms
data.body: Your hand, the table and the water you drink are all made of [[atom|atoms]]. Zoom in far enough on anything you can touch and you reach these tiny building blocks. Different things are just different atoms, joined in different ways. A skin cell, a drop of water and a grain of salt all come down to atoms.

shapes.text: each step down is far smaller than it looks

figure.altText: A hand, then a cell inside it, then a single tiny atom, joined by arrows that point from big to small.

data.title: What counts as matter?
data.body: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. A phone, an apple and a glass of water all do. So does air: it has mass, and it fills a balloon. Everything made of matter is made of atoms. Light and heat are different. They are energy, not matter.

shapes.text: all matter: they have mass and take up space

figure.altText: Pictures of air, water, a phone and an apple in a row, labelled as matter because they all have mass and take up space.

data.title: Even air, but not light
data.body: Air is made of atoms too, joined into tiny groups. But light and heat are not matter at all. They are forms of energy, so they are not made of atoms.

figure.altText: Two panels. On the left, pictures of air, water and a hand, labelled air, water and you, which are made of atoms. On the right, the sun and a flame, labelled light and heat, which are energy and not made of atoms.

data.task: Zoom in from your hand down to a single atom. Tap each stop.

stops.label: A hand
stops.note: You can see and hold this.

stops.label: A skin cell
stops.note: Too small to see without a microscope.

stops.label: A virus
stops.note: About 300 times smaller than the cell. It takes a strong microscope to see one.

stops.label: An atom
stops.sizeLabel: a few tenths of a nm
stops.note: About 300 times smaller again than a virus.

data.title: How wide is a hair?
data.body: Across one hair you could line up roughly a few hundred thousand atoms. A hair looks thin, yet it is hundreds of thousands of atoms wide.

shapes.text: hundreds of thousands fit across a hair

figure.altText: A strand of hair on the left and an arrow pointing to a single atom on the right, showing that hundreds of thousands of atoms fit across the width of one hair.

data.title: An idea before the proof
data.body: About 2,400 years ago the Greek thinker Democritus asked what would happen if you kept cutting something in half. He imagined a smallest piece that could not be cut, and called it atomos. Seeing atoms took far longer.

figure.altText: A bar cut in half again and again, getting smaller each time, ending in a tiny red piece: the idea of an atom as the piece you cannot cut.

data.speaker: npc-ada

data.title: Protons decide the element
data.body: The number of protons in an atom is its [[atomic-number|atomic number]]. One proton is always hydrogen. Two is always helium. Change the proton count and you have a different element.

figure.altText: Three things and their proton counts: a balloon filled with helium has 2 protons per atom, a diamond is carbon with 6, and a gold bar has 79.

data.task: Build an atom of oxygen. Oxygen has 8 protons, so tap + until it says so.
data.hint: Oxygen is element number 8. Watch the name change as you add protons.

data.title: The periodic table
data.body: The periodic table lists every element in order of atomic number. Each box shows the atomic number, the symbol and the name. Carbon, for example, is element 6 with the symbol C.

figure.altText: One box from the periodic table showing carbon: the atomic number 6 in the corner, the symbol C in the middle and the name Carbon underneath.

data.title: Atoms and ions
data.body: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. If an atom gains or loses electrons it becomes an ion with an electric charge. Its element does not change, because its protons did not change.

figure.altText: Two lithium particles side by side. A neutral atom with three protons and three electrons, and an ion that has lost one electron and so carries a positive charge.

data.title: Same element, different neutrons
data.body: Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons. These versions are called [[isotope|isotopes]]. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon, because both have 6 protons.

figure.altText: Two carbon atoms. Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons; carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons. Both have six electrons.

data.task: Make carbon-14 from carbon-12 by adding 2 neutrons.
data.hint: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons. Tap + two times to reach 8. It is still carbon.

data.title: Reading the name
data.body: The number after the name is the mass number: protons plus neutrons. Carbon has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons.

figure.altText: An equation: 6 protons plus 8 neutrons equals a mass number of 14, so the atom is called carbon-14.

data.title: Why your body can't tell
data.body: Chemistry is run by electrons, and isotopes of an element have the same electrons. So they behave almost identically in chemical reactions. That is why scientists can use a rare isotope as a tracer.

figure.altText: Two carbon atoms. Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons; carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons. Both have six electrons.

data.title: A centre and electrons
data.body: Every atom has a tiny centre called the [[nucleus]]. Around it are [[electron|electrons]]. Almost everything about an atom, including nearly all its mass, comes from that small centre.

figure.altText: An atom with a tiny nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons in the centre and 2 electrons on rings around it.

data.title: Three particles
data.body: The nucleus holds [[proton|protons]], which are positive, and [[neutron|neutrons]], which have no charge. Electrons are negative and sit outside the nucleus.

figure.altText: Three particles. A proton with a plus sign and a neutron with a zero, both in the nucleus, and an electron with a minus sign outside the nucleus.

data.task: Build a helium atom: 2 protons, 2 neutrons and 2 electrons.
data.hint: Add particles with the plus buttons. Helium has two of each.

data.speaker: npc-ada
data.title: The gold foil surprise
data.body: Ernest Rutherford's team fired tiny particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back. That could only happen if each atom had a tiny, dense centre: the nucleus.

figure.altText: Particles fired at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most pass straight through, but a few bounce back, showing there is something tiny and dense inside each atom.
figure.caption: Simplified and not to scale.

data.title: The stadium, answered
data.body: If an atom were a football stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a marble in the middle. Yet that marble holds nearly all of the stadium's mass.

shapes.text: a marble that holds nearly all the mass

figure.altText: A football stadium with a small marble at its centre, then an arrow to a marble: if an atom were a stadium, its nucleus would be a marble, which holds nearly all the mass.

data.title: Not tiny planets
data.body: Pictures often show electrons on neat rings, like planets. A better picture is a cloud: electrons are found in a region around the nucleus, and the cloud is where they are likely to be.

shapes.text: a cloud where electrons are likely to be found

figure.altText: A soft cloud shaded darker toward the centre with a tiny nucleus in the middle, showing where electrons are likely to be found.

data.title: A tug of war inside the nucleus
data.body: Protons push each other apart with an electric force. A stronger force, the strong force, pulls neighbouring particles together, but only at very short range. A nucleus lasts when the pull wins.

figure.altText: A nucleus with red arrows pointing outward, the electric push between protons, and blue arrows pointing inward, the strong force pulling the particles together.

data.task: Carbon-14 is unstable. Change the neutrons until the carbon atom is stable.
data.hint: Stable carbon has 6 or 7 neutrons. Tap - until the badge says Stable.

data.title: Neutrons are glue
data.body: Neutrons add pull from the strong force without adding any electric push. So a nucleus needs the right mix of protons and neutrons. Too few or too many neutrons and the nucleus is unstable.

figure.altText: Two carbon nuclei. Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons and is a balanced, stable nucleus. Carbon-14 has two extra neutrons and is out of balance, so it is unstable.

data.title: Unstable means it will change
data.body: An unstable nucleus does not last forever. At some moment it changes into a more stable nucleus and gives off [[radiation]]. A nucleus that does this is called radioactive.

figure.altText: An unstable nucleus on the left gives off radiation, shown by an arrow, and becomes a more stable nucleus on the right.

data.title: Found in a rock
data.body: Henri Becquerel left a uranium mineral on a wrapped photographic plate and found it fogged, even with no light. Radioactivity was discovered in a natural mineral, long before people made any nuclear technology.

figure.altText: A uranium mineral sitting above a photographic plate with dashed lines running down to it, showing invisible rays that left dark marks on the plate.
